# topic.editing

## Editing — beyond the basics

Notation, `C`, ids and the reads (outline · `view` + `parentId` · `search`) as `topic.index`; ids from its "Q3
launch plan" example — use your own reads' ids. Ops ride the prose `update` (ex.1's envelope: `ref` + `engine
"prose"` + `container` + `payload.ops`), several per call, applied in order. Examples ex.1–4 at the end.

- Every read prints `h='…'` (8 hex) per block = its content hash = what `ifHash` names (ex.2); `search` hits
  carry char ranges; `{"kind":"view","atRev":N}` = the doc at rev N (ex.4).

- Keep up to date (people edit the doc while you work and between your turns — assume it changed):
  - Bookmark = the last `rev` you saw (every read and write ack returns it). A later turn that touches the doc
    starts with `read( …, payload = {"kind":"view","sinceRev":12} )` (12 = the bookmark) → only the blocks
    changed since (unchanged runs fold into `<gap/>`, deleted blocks show `<gone id=…/>`), fresh ids and `h`;
    act on those, no full re-read. Between your own consecutive writes no read: the ack (`rev`, `session`, the
    `xml` of what you wrote) anchors the next call.
  - `guard_mismatch` = someone changed that block after your read; the refusal shows it as it stands. Their
    words win: a placeholder you were filling now holds their text → drop that op (add yours beneath theirs only if
    it still adds something; say you kept their text); your pending block is gone (`block_gone`, `data.op`
    "remove") → they do not want that section: drop it, never re-create it; a block you were rewriting → fold
    their new words into yours, guarded on the new `h`. Never your text over theirs, never resend with force.
    `find_none` / `char_gone` on words you quoted = the same: read that block, work with what it says now.
  - A read shows a person as `<mention user label? self?/>` (`self='true'` = the person you act for): mention
    someone else only with that `user` id; outside the doc write `@` + the label, else "@[person]".
  - Comments: `query( … )` again with `"afterSeq": <last seq you saw>` → only newer comments, replies, resolves.

- Asked to add or expand sections of an existing doc → plant the plan first (WHILE THEY WATCH): ONE `insert` at the spot
  (`"side":"after"` a block id, or `{"kind":"root"}` + `"side":"end"`) whose markdown is `<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>`
  with `"blocks":{"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Risks: what could slip and the fallback"},"s2":{…}}`; then fill each as
  after a birth: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body.
- Rewrite a block = `replace` by id (ex.1): `"as":"markdown"` re-creates it, chips and all (chip map `blocks`
  BESIDE `from`); `"as":"text"` re-words in place, refused on a block holding a chip (→ find-target the words,
  or markdown). `"ifHash"` = the block's `h`, on EVERY `replace`/`delete` of a block someone else wrote (one
  you just wrote: `"ifRev":<your last ack's rev>`; a bare one is refused `missing_guard` — a pending block's fill
  or withdrawal needs none; `"force":true` only when told to overwrite); `guard_mismatch` = changed since your
  read → never resend with force (Keep up to date, above); find/chars targets take NO `ifHash` (the words / ids
  are the guard; else `unknown_key`).
- `anchors_affected` refusal = the change removes words a comment hangs on → narrow the edit around those words
  (target the rest by `find`), or ask in that thread whether they should go; `"allowDetach":true` beside `"op"`
  (never on the payload) only when a person asked for the passage to go → the thread stays, detached (ack
  notices); tell the user. NEVER for the thread you are answering (refused regardless): reply there, resolve
  it, then edit.
- In-doc link: `[Intro](#<bid>)` = heading block id off a read/ack (a `~slug` the viewer appends stays); heading
  born in the same fill → `[Intro](#intro)` (GFM slug).
- `delete` (ex.1): find target = exactly the quoted words, leading space included (so none doubles up), or a block
  id + `ifHash`, several ids + `"ifRev"` (a list or table goes whole: items, rows, their ids); never `replace` with empty content (refused).
  A tab keeps one block: deleting its LAST is refused (`last_block`) — to clear a tab, `replace` that block (same guard) with
  `<?claude block empty?>` (+ `"blocks":{"empty":{"type":"paragraph"}}`), the one empty paragraph an editor leaves.
- `move` (ex.1): block ids + `to` = an insert target + `side` (`{"kind":"root"}` + `"end"` = bottom of the tab).
- List kind in place (items, ids, threads stay): `set` `"attrs":{"kind":"bullet"|"ordered"|"check"}` on the list
  id (ex.2); tick an item: `"attrs":{"checked":true}` on its listItem id. Never delete + re-insert a list for
  this (retires every id in it, detaches its comments).
- Table rows (ex.2): `insert` `"as":"blocks"`, every cell spelled, one per column; `side` `"end"` on the table id
  → appended, `"after"` + a row id → below that row. A cell's words: find → `replace` `"as":"text"`; the whole
  table `"as":"markdown"` works too but re-types every row. Whole cell: `replace` + the cell target
  (topic.index IDS) + `"with"` + `"ifRev":<rev of the read row/col came from, not a later ack's>` (bare →
  `missing_guard`) — rows/columns changed since → refused `guard_mismatch` + the table's shape now: re-aim, resend.
- Table column (ex.3): ONE `insert`, `"each":true` = a copy of the source at EVERY listed row id (≤ 4,096 a
  call); `side` `"end"` | `"start"` → last | first column, or each row's neighbour cell + `"after"` | `"before"`;
  header row → header cell; `""` = blank cell; words fill every copy alike. An id twice → `same_anchor`; several
  ids without `"each"` → `place_arity`. Remove a column: ONE `delete` naming every cell of it + `"ifRev"` (your read's
  `rev`).
- Deleted text is in the doc's history — never retype it or ask for it (ex.4): `atRev` read (step back until the
  text is there; `latest` = the rev now), then re-insert the words with an ordinary `insert`; or `restore`, the
  only op in its call, `payload.ifRev` = that `latest` → rewinds the whole tab, only when nothing else changed
  since.

### Examples

ex.1 — one call, in order: words out by quote · bullets + a link after a block · guarded rewrite with chips ·
guarded delete of a whole list · the table to the bottom:
```
update( ref = {"object":"node","id":"be1476b2-62c1"}, engine = "prose", container = C, payload = {"ops":[
  {"op":"delete","target":{"kind":"find","text":" if legal review runs long"}},
  {"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.16"]},"side":"after",
   "source":{"as":"markdown","from":{"kind":"inline","content":"- Launch retro on Oct 6\n- [Vendor pricing](https://example.com/pricing)"}}},
  {"op":"replace","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.16"]},"ifHash":"cddc588b",
   "with":{"as":"markdown","blocks":{"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"due":{"type":"date","value":"2026-10-06"}},
           "from":{"kind":"inline","content":"Owner <?claude block me?>, launch moved to <?claude block due?>."}}},
  {"op":"delete","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.60"]},"ifHash":"1d9a3f0c"},
  {"op":"move","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.90"]},"to":{"target":{"kind":"root"},"side":"end"}} ]} )
```
ex.2 — one table read whole, then a row appended and a list made a checklist:
```
read( …, payload = {"kind":"view","parentId":"mq2x81a0kfd.90"} )
→ <doc rev='12' …><table id='mq2x81a0kfd.90' h='c8d95136'><row id='.91' h='89de16c2'><cell id='.92' header='true'>… <row id='.123' …>…
update( …, payload = {"ops":[
  {"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.90"]},"side":"end",
   "source":{"as":"blocks","from":{"kind":"inline","content":[{"type":"row","content":[
     {"type":"cell","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Oct 6"}]}]},
     {"type":"cell","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Launch retro"}]}]}]}]}}},
  {"op":"set","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.40"]},"attrs":{"kind":"check"}} ]} )
```
ex.3 — a column = a blank cell at the end of EVERY row (row ids from the view):
```
{"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.91","mq2x81a0kfd.123"]},"side":"end","each":true,
 "source":{"as":"text","from":{"kind":"inline","content":""}}}
```
ex.4 — bring back: `read( …, payload = {"kind":"view","atRev":9} )` → rev 9 of the doc as it read then, `latest: 14` (the
rev now) beside the xml → re-insert the words (an `insert` as in ex.1), or rewind:
`update( …, payload = {"ifRev":14,"ops":[{"op":"restore","rev":9}]} )`.

## What is Thunderjar

Thunderjar is a benchmarking framework for measuring how well AI coding agents perform on software engineering tasks. It runs an agent against a codebase, then evaluates the result against a set of defined measurements.

See `docs/terminology.md` for the full glossary. Key concepts:

- **Task** — a starting commit + a prompt. Defines what the agent is asked to do and from what state.
- **Prompt** — a named, reusable configuration that installs prompt files into the worktree via a shell command (e.g. `cp prompts/skills.md CLAUDE.md`). Referenced by ID.
- **Experiment** — a named comparison: one task × arrays of variable values (models, harnesses, prompts). Produces one run per permutation.
- **Run** — a single execution under one specific combination of variable values. Uses a git worktree so runs are isolated.
- **Measurements** — assertions evaluated after a run (file created, grep present/absent, command exit code, correctness test). Defined on the task; the result of a run is the set of measurement outcomes.

  # not yet implemented

  thunderjar.config.ts
  prompts/
  output/

=== docs/test_measure_proposal.md
## Test measurement proposal (template-driven)

### Summary

We want a built-in measurer that can validate correctness by **materialising a test file from a template into the worktree**, then **running a test command**, then **capturing the result as a measure**.

This is distinct from “tests pass” (which is just `commandExitCode` against a repo’s normal test suite). This measurer is for *targeted* correctness checks that can be applied across tasks, even if the repo doesn’t already contain the relevant test.

### Terminology alignment

- **measurer**: reusable evaluator definition
- **measurement**: task-level application of a measurer (may be named/id’ed)
- **measure**: the outcome/value produced by running a measurement (stored in results)

### Lifecycle (intended execution order)

1. Worktree is created
2. Agent/harness runs (modifies repo)
3. Measurements are applied sequentially (one by one)
4. When the runner reaches a “test template” measurement:
   - write the templated test file into the worktree
   - run a test command targeting that file (or a configured runner)
   - capture stdout/stderr/exitCode and store as the measure

### Name ideas (best-first)

- `templateTest` (recommended): describes what it does without colliding with “harness”
- `fixtureTest`: common term, but slightly less explicit than “template”
- `goldenTest`: only if we decide this is “golden/snapshot” oriented
- `correctnessTest`: aligns with existing legacy measurement type name `correctness-test`

Notes:
- Avoid `harnessTest` (confuses with the “harness” concept).
- If we keep the legacy measurement type `correctness-test`, the measurer can still be named `templateTest` (or vice versa); we can map between them in the builder/runner for backwards compatibility.

### Proposed measurement config shape

Minimum viable config:
- `templatePath`: where to read the template from (within the repo/config context)
- `outputPath`: where to write the generated test file in the worktree
- `run` (optional): command to execute (defaults TBD)
- `expectedExitCode` (optional): default `0`

Example (conceptual):

```ts
{
  measurementId: "add_function_correctness",
  measurerName: "templateTest",
  config: {
    templatePath: "evaluation-sandbox/tests/add.test.ts.template",
    outputPath: "test/add.test.ts",
    run: "bun test test/add.test.ts",
    expectedExitCode: 0,
  }
}
```

### Measure/result shape (what gets recorded)

Recommended stored value for this measurer:

```ts
{
  exitCode: number,
  stdout: string,
  stderr: string
}
```

Pass/fail is derived from `exitCode === expectedExitCode` (default expectedExitCode=0).

### Open questions / decisions

- **Template substitution**: are templates copied verbatim, or do we support placeholder substitution (e.g. `{taskId}`, `{worktreePath}`, `{measurementId}`, etc.)?
- **Default `run`**: do we default to `config.commands.testRunner` (repo-level), or require an explicit `run` that targets the generated file?
- **Cleanup**: do we keep generated tests committed in the worktree, or treat them as temporary artifacts only used for measurement?
- **Working directory**: should test execution run in `worktreePath` or `commands.harnessWorkingDirectory`?

=== docs/regular-usage-workflow.md
# Regular Usage Workflow

How everyday BAU work turns into Thunderjar tasks.

## The three scenarios

**Scenario 1 — clean one-shot.** You give the agent a task ("there's an X bug, can you solve it?") and it nails it. You say "looks great, thanks." Good candidate.

**Scenario 2 — one-shot with a correction.** Same as above, but you had to say "you missed Y" once, the agent fixed it, and then you were satisfied. Still a good candidate — the task was one-shot-*able*, the current model/prompt combo just fell short of it. That gap is exactly what's worth capturing.

Within Scenario 2, "you missed Y" splits into two kinds, and they get fixed differently:

- **Convention gap** — e.g. "you didn't write a test." Not something a real bug report should have needed to say; the fix belongs in a Prompt Set (CLAUDE.md / skills), not the task instruction. The task instruction is left untouched; you iterate on Prompt Sets to see which one gets the agent to do it unprompted.
- **Specification gap** — e.g. "there's other buggy/edge-case behavior you missed." The original instruction was an incomplete bug report — no amount of prompt tuning teaches an agent to guess an edge case nobody mentioned. Fix this by rewriting the task instruction to include the missing detail, as a real complete bug report would. Once corrected, treat it like Scenario 1 — there's nothing left to iterate on.

**Scenario 3 — needs ongoing steering.** The task requires iterative back-and-forth, judgment calls the instruction couldn't have anticipated, multiple rounds of direction. This never ends in a clean "looks great" — it just resolves through negotiation. **Not a Thunderjar candidate.** Don't try to write measurements for it and don't try to prompt-tune your way out of it; the task itself is the wrong shape for one-shot benchmarking.

## Mechanics of creating measurements (Scenarios 1 and 2)

1. Work happens on ordinary commits, not a Thunderjar worktree. `A` = the pre-feature commit, `B/C/D` = the feature work (may take several commits to land, including any Scenario 2 correction).
2. Once satisfied, mine measurements from the `A..D` diff: what files should exist, what should NOT be present (e.g. `as any`), and — most importantly — a `correctness-test` template capturing the actual contract (independent of whether the agent's own tests are any good). Commit this as `E`.
3. Create a new branch off `A` and cherry-pick `E` onto it. That tip commit — `A`'s codebase plus `E`'s measurements, but never `B/C/D`'s actual solution — becomes the Task's permanent `commitHash`. A worktree checked out here has the measurements already present but has to solve the problem from scratch.
4. For Scenario 2's specification gaps: rewrite the task instruction before banking it (see above) rather than keeping the original incomplete prompt around.
5. For Scenario 2's convention gaps: no instruction change. Instead, iterate on Prompt Sets — improve the CLAUDE.md/skills content (ordinary commits on `main`, e.g. commit `F`), then re-run the experiment against the same pinned `commitHash` with the new Prompt Set to see if it closes the gap. Prompt Sets are applied via `git checkout <ref> -- <pathspec>` inside the worktree, which reaches the shared object database regardless of which commit the worktree itself is pinned to — so `F`, `G`, `H`... keep landing on ordinary `main` and get picked up without ever re-pinning the task.

## Two mechanisms still needed

**Detecting Scenario 1/2 (a skill or a hook).** Something needs to notice "this session just ended in success, is this a good Thunderjar candidate?" and prompt the user to walk through turning it into a task. Whether this is a hook that watches every turn and proactively nudges, or a skill the user invokes themselves in the moment, is not yet decided.

**Creating the measurements (a skill).** Something needs to help turn a known-good `A..D` diff into the actual measurement set — proposing `fileCreated`/`grep`/`command` assertions and, most valuably, drafting the `correctness-test` template — for the human to review before it's committed as `E`.
=== docs/harness-vs-models.md
# Harness vs Models — Design Decision

The current `variables: { models, harnesses, prompts }` structure generates all permutations, which produces invalid combinations — e.g. `opencode` with a claude model ID, or `claude-code` with an opencode model ID.

## Option A — harness+model as explicit pairs (`agents`)

```typescript
variables: {
  agents: [
    { harness: 'claude-code', model: 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001' },
    { harness: 'opencode', model: 'opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free' },
  ],
  prompts: ['snerk', 'glurk'],
}
```

Permutations become `agents × prompts`. Explicit, no invalid combos possible.

## Option B — models nested under each harness

```typescript
variables: {
  harnesses: {
    'claude-code': ['claude-haiku-4-5-20251001'],
    'opencode': ['opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free', 'opencode/north-mini'],
  },
  prompts: ['snerk', 'glurk'],
}
```

Permutations become `(harness × its models) × prompts`. More compact when comparing many models within the same harness.

## Preference

Option A is the more honest representation of what a run actually is (one agent, one prompt) and makes it easier to read what will be compared. Option B is more compact for multi-model-per-harness comparisons.
=== docs/operating_principles.md
# Operating Principles

## Prefer callbacks over static values

Throughout the builder API, configuration that could be a plain string is instead a callback returning a string. For example, `onWorktreeCreate`, harness `cli`, and measurer `evaluate` are all functions rather than raw values.

The reason: callbacks receive a context object. As the framework evolves, more values can be added to that context object and made available to callers without breaking existing configurations. A plain string can never be given new information; a callback always can.

This applies consistently across the API — when in doubt, make it a callback.

=== docs/paned-runner-display.md
# Paned runner display

## Problem

The current live display in `runExperiment` uses raw ANSI cursor-up rewrites on the normal screen buffer. Harness subprocess stdout flows directly to the terminal and corrupts the cursor position, causing the progress view to jump and break.

## Proposed design

Replace the raw ANSI display with a full-screen paned layout using **ink** (React-based TUI). Each permutation gets its own bounded pane. All harness output is captured and routed into that pane only.

When there are too many variations to tile usefully, fall back to a compact list view.

---

## Layout algorithm

Rather than a fixed breakpoint table, the layout is computed from the actual terminal size at render time:

1. Define minimum viable pane dimensions (e.g. `MIN_W = 35`, `MIN_H = 6`)
2. `maxCols = floor(termWidth / MIN_W)`, `maxRows = floor(termHeight / MIN_H)`
3. If `N > maxCols × maxRows` → **list mode** (see below)
4. Otherwise, find the column count that produces the most square grid:
   - Try each `cols` from 1 to `maxCols`
   - `rows = ceil(N / cols)`
   - Pick the `cols` where `(paneWidth / paneHeight)` is closest to a target aspect ratio (~2.5 to account for character cell proportions)

This means a wide terminal naturally gets more columns, a tall terminal gets more rows, and the layout reflows instantly on resize.

## Architecture

### New file: `src/cli/RunnerDisplay.tsx`

ink React component. Owns all pane state. Accepts a `permutations` list and an `onReady` callback:

```ts
interface RunCallbacks {
  onOutput: (permIndex: number, line: string) => void;

}

## Test measurement proposal (template-driven)

### Summary

We want a built-in measurer that can validate correctness by **materialising a test file from a template into the worktree**, then **running a test command**, then **capturing the result as a measure**.

This is distinct from “tests pass” (which is just `commandExitCode` against a repo’s normal test suite). This measurer is for *targeted* correctness checks that can be applied across tasks, even if the repo doesn’t already contain the relevant test.

### Terminology alignment

- **measurer**: reusable evaluator definition
- **measurement**: task-level application of a measurer (may be named/id’ed)
- **measure**: the outcome/value produced by running a measurement (stored in results)

### Lifecycle (intended execution order)

1. Worktree is created
2. Agent/harness runs (modifies repo)
3. Measurements are applied sequentially (one by one)
4. When the runner reaches a “test template” measurement:
   - write the templated test file into the worktree
   - run a test command targeting that file (or a configured runner)
   - capture stdout/stderr/exitCode and store as the measure

### Name ideas (best-first)

- `templateTest` (recommended): describes what it does without colliding with “harness”
- `fixtureTest`: common term, but slightly less explicit than “template”
- `goldenTest`: only if we decide this is “golden/snapshot” oriented
- `correctnessTest`: aligns with existing legacy measurement type name `correctness-test`

Notes:
- Avoid `harnessTest` (confuses with the “harness” concept).
- If we keep the legacy measurement type `correctness-test`, the measurer can still be named `templateTest` (or vice versa); we can map between them in the builder/runner for backwards compatibility.

### Proposed measurement config shape

Minimum viable config:
- `templatePath`: where to read the template from (within the repo/config context)
- `outputPath`: where to write the generated test file in the worktree
- `run` (optional): command to execute (defaults TBD)
- `expectedExitCode` (optional): default `0`

Example (conceptual):

```ts
{
  measurementId: "add_function_correctness",
  measurerName: "templateTest",
  config: {
    templatePath: "evaluation-sandbox/tests/add.test.ts.template",
    outputPath: "test/add.test.ts",
    run: "bun test test/add.test.ts",
    expectedExitCode: 0,
  }
}
```

### Measure/result shape (what gets recorded)

Recommended stored value for this measurer:

```ts
{
  exitCode: number,
  stdout: string,
  stderr: string
}
```

Pass/fail is derived from `exitCode === expectedExitCode` (default expectedExitCode=0).

### Open questions / decisions

- **Template substitution**: are templates copied verbatim, or do we support placeholder substitution (e.g. `{taskId}`, `{worktreePath}`, `{measurementId}`, etc.)?
- **Default `run`**: do we default to `config.commands.testRunner` (repo-level), or require an explicit `run` that targets the generated file?
- **Cleanup**: do we keep generated tests committed in the worktree, or treat them as temporary artifacts only used for measurement?
- **Working directory**: should test execution run in `worktreePath` or `commands.harnessWorkingDirectory`?

=== docs/regular-usage-workflow.md
# Regular Usage Workflow

How everyday BAU work turns into Thunderjar tasks.

## The three scenarios

**Scenario 1 — clean one-shot.** You give the agent a task ("there's an X bug, can you solve it?") and it nails it. You say "looks great, thanks." Good candidate.

**Scenario 2 — one-shot with a correction.** Same as above, but you had to say "you missed Y" once, the agent fixed it, and then you were satisfied. Still a good candidate — the task was one-shot-*able*, the current model/prompt combo just fell short of it. That gap is exactly what's worth capturing.

Within Scenario 2, "you missed Y" splits into two kinds, and they get fixed differently:

- **Convention gap** — e.g. "you didn't write a test." Not something a real bug report should have needed to say; the fix belongs in a Prompt Set (CLAUDE.md / skills), not the task instruction. The task instruction is left untouched; you iterate on Prompt Sets to see which one gets the agent to do it unprompted.
- **Specification gap** — e.g. "there's other buggy/edge-case behavior you missed." The original instruction was an incomplete bug report — no amount of prompt tuning teaches an agent to guess an edge case nobody mentioned. Fix this by rewriting the task instruction to include the missing detail, as a real complete bug report would. Once corrected, treat it like Scenario 1 — there's nothing left to iterate on.

**Scenario 3 — needs ongoing steering.** The task requires iterative back-and-forth, judgment calls the instruction couldn't have anticipated, multiple rounds of direction. This never ends in a clean "looks great" — it just resolves through negotiation. **Not a Thunderjar candidate.** Don't try to write measurements for it and don't try to prompt-tune your way out of it; the task itself is the wrong shape for one-shot benchmarking.

## Mechanics of creating measurements (Scenarios 1 and 2)

1. Work happens on ordinary commits, not a Thunderjar worktree. `A` = the pre-feature commit, `B/C/D` = the feature work (may take several commits to land, including any Scenario 2 correction).
2. Once satisfied, mine measurements from the `A..D` diff: what files should exist, what should NOT be present (e.g. `as any`), and — most importantly — a `correctness-test` template capturing the actual contract (independent of whether the agent's own tests are any good). Commit this as `E`.
3. Create a new branch off `A` and cherry-pick `E` onto it. That tip commit — `A`'s codebase plus `E`'s measurements, but never `B/C/D`'s actual solution — becomes the Task's permanent `commitHash`. A worktree checked out here has the measurements already present but has to solve the problem from scratch.
4. For Scenario 2's specification gaps: rewrite the task instruction before banking it (see above) rather than keeping the original incomplete prompt around.
5. For Scenario 2's convention gaps: no instruction change. Instead, iterate on Prompt Sets — improve the CLAUDE.md/skills content (ordinary commits on `main`, e.g. commit `F`), then re-run the experiment against the same pinned `commitHash` with the new Prompt Set to see if it closes the gap. Prompt Sets are applied via `git checkout <ref> -- <pathspec>` inside the worktree, which reaches the shared object database regardless of which commit the worktree itself is pinned to — so `F`, `G`, `H`... keep landing on ordinary `main` and get picked up without ever re-pinning the task.

## Two mechanisms still needed

**Detecting Scenario 1/2 (a skill or a hook).** Something needs to notice "this session just ended in success, is this a good Thunderjar candidate?" and prompt the user to walk through turning it into a task. Whether this is a hook that watches every turn and proactively nudges, or a skill the user invokes themselves in the moment, is not yet decided.

**Creating the measurements (a skill).** Something needs to help turn a known-good `A..D` diff into the actual measurement set — proposing `fileCreated`/`grep`/`command` assertions and, most valuably, drafting the `correctness-test` template — for the human to review before it's committed as `E`.
=== docs/harness-vs-models.md
# Harness vs Models — Design Decision

The current `variables: { models, harnesses, prompts }` structure generates all permutations, which produces invalid combinations — e.g. `opencode` with a claude model ID, or `claude-code` with an opencode model ID.

## Option A — harness+model as explicit pairs (`agents`)

```typescript
variables: {
  agents: [
    { harness: 'claude-code', model: 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001' },
    { harness: 'opencode', model: 'opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free' },
  ],
  prompts: ['snerk', 'glurk'],
}
```

Permutations become `agents × prompts`. Explicit, no invalid combos possible.

## Option B — models nested under each harness

```typescript
variables: {
  harnesses: {
    'claude-code': ['claude-haiku-4-5-20251001'],
    'opencode': ['opencode/deepseek-v4-flash-free', 'opencode/north-mini'],
  },
  prompts: ['snerk', 'glurk'],
}
```

Permutations become `(harness × its models) × prompts`. More compact when comparing many models within the same harness.

## Preference

Option A is the more honest representation of what a run actually is (one agent, one prompt) and makes it easier to read what will be compared. Option B is more compact for multi-model-per-harness comparisons.
=== docs/operating_principles.md
# Operating Principles

## Prefer callbacks over static values

Throughout the builder API, configuration that could be a plain string is instead a callback returning a string. For example, `onWorktreeCreate`, harness `cli`, and measurer `evaluate` are all functions rather than raw values.

The reason: callbacks receive a context object. As the framework evolves, more values can be added to that context object and made available to callers without breaking existing configurations. A plain string can never be given new information; a callback always can.

This applies consistently across the API — when in doubt, make it a callback.

The current live display in `runExperiment` uses raw ANSI cursor-up rewrites on the normal screen buffer. Harness subprocess stdout flows directly to the terminal and corrupts the cursor position, causing the progress view to jump and break.

┌─ p-b/haiku/cc ●1:18 ─┐┌─ p-a/son/oc ─ ●1:52 ─┐┌─ p-b/son/oc ─ ● 2:01 ─┐┌─ p-a/opus/oc ─ ● 1:44 ─┐┌─ p-b/opus/oc ─ ● 0:37 ─┐
│                       ││                        ││                         ││                          ││                          │
│  working...           ││  working...            ││  working...             ││  working...              ││  working...              │
└───────────────────────┘└────────────────────────┘└─────────────────────────┘└─────────────────────────┘└──────────────────────────┘
```

---

## List mode

Triggered when `N > maxCols × maxRows` for the minimum pane size. Shows:

- A summary header: `Running N variations... X/N complete` + a count-up timer
- One line per variation with: name, status icon, elapsed time, and error note if failed
- Variations sorted: complete/failed first (in finish order), then running ones

```
Running 100 variations...
12/100 complete                                             0:08:44

prompt-a / sonnet / claude-code      ✓   42s
prompt-b / sonnet / claude-code      ✓   38s
prompt-a / opus / claude-code        ✗   61s  (exit 1)
prompt-b / opus / claude-code        ✓   55s
prompt-a / haiku / claude-code       ✓   29s
...
prompt-x / opus / opencode           ●  1:14
prompt-y / haiku / opencode          ●  0:52
```

---

## Pane anatomy

**While running:**
```
┌─ prompt-a / claude-sonnet-4-6 / claude-code ──── ● 1:23 ─┐
│                                                            │
│  working...                                                │
│                                                            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**On completion:**
```
┌─ prompt-a / claude-sonnet-4-6 / claude-code ──── ✓ 1:47 ─┐
│ Task completed successfully.                               │
│ Created src/components/Button.tsx                          │
│ Modified src/index.ts                                      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Header:** status icon (● running / ✓ complete / ✗ failed), label, elapsed time
- **Body (running):** static "working..." placeholder
- **Body (done):** final stdout/stderr from the harness, truncated to pane width and height
- **Border:** ink `borderStyle="single"`; colour changes on completion (green) or failure (red)

---

## Architecture

### New file: `src/cli/RunnerDisplay.tsx`

ink React component. Owns all pane state. Accepts a `permutations` list and an `onReady` callback:

```ts
interface RunCallbacks {
  onOutput: (permIndex: number, line: string) => void;
  onStatusChange: (permIndex: number, status: 'running' | 'complete' | 'failed') => void;
}

<RunnerDisplay permutations={RunPermutation[]} onReady={(cb: RunCallbacks) => void} />
```

On mount, the component calls `onReady(callbacks)` to hand control back to the runner. The runner drives state via callbacks; ink re-renders reactively.

Two sub-components:
- `<TileView>` — renders the pane grid when tiling is viable
- `<ListView>` — renders the compact list when there are too many variations

### Modified: `src/runner.ts`

- `runExperiment` gains a `callbacks: RunCallbacks` parameter; all existing ANSI display code is removed
- Harness subprocess stays as `Bun.$` — stdout/stderr are captured from the completed result and pushed to the pane via `onOutput`
- `generatePermutations` is exported so the CLI can compute permutations before mounting the display

1549:        "text": "For grpc, the OpenTelemetry SDK reads the standard OTLP variables directly, so existing configurations that set the per-signal metrics variables continue to work. The following environment variables control which attributes are included in metrics to manage cardinality: Lower cardinality generally means better performance and lower storage costs but less granular data for analysis. Distributed tracing exports spans that link each user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers, so you can view a full request as a single trace in your tracing backend. Tracing is off by default. To enable it, set both CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1, then set OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER to choose where spans are sent.",
1629:        "text": "The last three control granularity. Without them, you get spans and timings but not the content. With them, you get prompt text, tool parameters, and full tool input/output in your traces. Privacy note: Those last three flags mean your prompts and tool outputs end up in your Tempo instance. Fine for local development. Think carefully before pointing this at a shared collector. Layer 2: ~/.claude/settings.json controls where telemetry goes. Add an env block with standard OTel SDK environment variables: ... These are standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables. The env key in settings.json injects them into the Claude Code process. You could set them in your shell instead, but settings.json keeps them scoped to Claude and out of your global environment. Say hello to Claude code in the terminal. Open Grafana at http://localhost:3000. Navigate to Explore, select the Tempo data source, and search for recent traces.",
1661:        "text": "Five separate variables control whether the actual content of a session leaves the machine, and they are deliberately separate because they carry different risk. Logging tool details is a reasonable audit control. Logging user prompts and assistant responses means your collector now holds the conversation, and your collector's retention policy is now your AI data-retention policy. # Content logging is opt-in, per kind, and each of these is a # policy decision rather than a configuration one. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 # the actual prompt text OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 # the actual model responses OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 # tool parameters, commands, skill names OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 # tool input/output \u2014 requires tracing OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES=1 # or file:<dir> to write bodies to disk CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_CONTENT_MAX_LENGTH=61440 # default, UTF-16 code units # Cardinality controls, with their DEFAULTS shown. Session id # is on by default, which is the one to think about at scale.",

3027:    "text": "That's exactly the right shape for it, and dependency injection is a good name for the pattern too. The test case doesn't hard-code a real GitHub MCP server, it specifies an interface, a GitHub-shaped MCP, and Thunderjar's container setup swaps in whichever implementation matches the run, a real one for actual production validation, a fake or mock one that just records what calls were made and returns canned responses for routine automated testing.\n\nThat actually solves two problems at once, it keeps your hundred parallel runs safe and side-effect-free like we just discussed, and it gives you a clean new assertion surface, since the fake MCP can log every call it received, so you're no longer just checking file state or commits, you can assert did it call create-pull-request with these exact arguments, which is arguably a much more direct signal for that specific agentic flow than inferring intent from git history alone.",
3226:    "text": "Right, so this is a step removed from what we've been designing \u2014 now we're talking about how you'd get confidence that Thunderjar itself, the orchestrator, works correctly, separate from the coding-agent runs it's orchestrating.\n\nThat naturally splits into a few layers, and they want pretty different testing strategies.\n\nThe core logic \u2014 building the matrix of permutations from your config, generating the right git checkout commands, constructing Docker image tags, parsing the structured JSON result object into your summary format \u2014 that's all pure-ish functions with predictable inputs and outputs, so ordinary unit tests, no Docker involved at all. That's the bulk of your test coverage and the cheapest to run.\n\nThe Docker orchestration layer \u2014 actually spinning up containers, running them, committing them, pushing to a registry \u2014 is where it gets more interesting, because you probably don't want every CI run of Thunderjar's own test suite to spin up real Claude Code sessions burning real API cost against real models. So this is a natural seam for exactly the dependency-injection pattern you landed on earlier for MCP servers, an abstraction over \"container runtime\" and \"coding agent invocation\" that in tests gets swapped for a fake, a container that just echoes back a canned result object instantly, so you can test \"did Thunderjar correctly parse this JSON and build this summary\" without any Docker daemon or API call actually happening.\n\nThen a smaller number of true integration tests, maybe just a handful, that do run a real trivial Docker container end to end, to catch the things a mock can't, like whether your actual `docker commit` and tagging shell-out code works against a real daemon.\n\nIs the CLI itself using something like `commander` or is it built on a lower-level arg-parsing setup, that'll shape how you approach testing the command surface itself?",
3316:    "text": "That's a clean way to get real coverage without real API calls, treat \"fake harness\" as just another entry in the same harness-config mechanism, not a special test-only code path bolted on separately.\n\nSo concretely, the config that says \"harness equals Claude Code, invoke it via `claude -p`\" is structurally identical to a config that says \"harness equals fake, invoke it via `node fake-agent.js`,\" same interface, same expected output shape, JSON result object with usage, cost, session ID, whatever. That means your integration tests get to exercise the entire real pipeline, image build, container start, wait, commit, push, parse \u2014 using nothing but that fake harness, and the only thing you're mocking is the one genuinely expensive, non-deterministic, external-dependency step. Everything downstream of \"container produced a result\" is tested completely for real.\n\nAnd it doubles as a nice authoring tool too, since you could write a handful of fake harness scripts that deliberately produce edge cases, one that never commits, one that produces a malformed JSON result, one that times out, to test that your measurement and reporting layer handles those failure modes correctly, which is much harder to reliably trigger with a real model.",

1549:        "text": "For grpc, the OpenTelemetry SDK reads the standard OTLP variables directly, so existing configurations that set the per-signal metrics variables continue to work. On machines with managed settings, Claude Code may remove developer-set per-signal credentials and endpoints at startup. The following environment variables control which attributes are included in metrics to manage cardinality: Lower cardinality generally means better performance and lower storage costs but less granular data for analysis. Distributed tracing exports spans that link each user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers, so you can view a full request as a single trace in your tracing backend. Tracing is off by default. To enable it, set both CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1, then set OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER to choose where spans are sent.",
1629:        "text": "The last three control granularity. Without them, you get spans and timings but not the content. With them, you get prompt text, tool parameters, and full tool input/output in your traces. Privacy note: Those last three flags mean your prompts and tool outputs end up in your Tempo instance. Fine for local development. Think carefully before pointing this at a shared collector. Layer 2: ~/.claude/settings.json controls where telemetry goes. Add an env block with standard OTel SDK environment variables: ... These are standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables. The env key in settings.json injects them into the Claude Code process. You could set them in your shell instead, but settings.json keeps them scoped to Claude and out of your global environment. Say hello to Claude code in the terminal. Open Grafana at http://localhost:3000. Navigate to Explore, select the Tempo data source, and search for recent traces.",
1661:        "text": "Five separate variables control whether the actual content of a session leaves the machine, and they are deliberately separate because they carry different risk. Logging tool details is a reasonable audit control. Logging user prompts and assistant responses means your collector now holds the conversation, and your collector's retention policy is now your AI data-retention policy. # Content logging is opt-in, per kind, and each of these is a # policy decision rather than a configuration one. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 # the actual prompt text OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 # the actual model responses OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 # tool parameters, commands, skill names OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 # tool input/output \u2014 requires tracing OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES=1 # or file:<dir> to write bodies to disk CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_CONTENT_MAX_LENGTH=61440 # default, UTF-16 code units # Cardinality controls, with their DEFAULTS shown. Session id # is on by default, which is the one to think about at scale.",
1988:    "text": "Actually easier than you might expect, in principle. 3027:    "text": "That's exactly the right shape for it, and dependency injection is a good name for the pattern too. The test case doesn't hard-code a real GitHub MCP server, it specifies an interface, a GitHub-shaped MCP, and Thunderjar's container setup swaps in whichever implementation matches the run, a real one for actual production validation, a fake or mock one that just records what calls were made and returns canned responses for routine automated testing.\n\nThat actually solves two problems at once, it keeps your hundred parallel runs safe and side-effect-free like we just discussed, and it gives you a clean new assertion surface, since the fake MCP can log every call it received, so you're no longer just checking file state or commits, you can assert did it call create-pull-request with these exact arguments, which is arguably a much more direct signal for that specific agentic flow than inferring intent from git history alone.",
3226:    "text": "Right, so this is a step removed from what we've been designing \u2014 now we're talking about how you'd get confidence that Thunderjar itself, the orchestrator, works correctly, separate from the coding-agent runs it's orchestrating.\n\nThat naturally splits into a few layers, and they want pretty different testing strategies.\n\nThe core logic \u2014 building the matrix of permutations from your config, generating the right git checkout commands, constructing Docker image tags, parsing the structured JSON result object into your summary format \u2014 that's all pure-ish functions with predictable inputs and outputs, so ordinary unit tests, no Docker involved at all. 3316:    "text": "That's a clean way to get real coverage without real API calls, treat \"fake harness\" as just another entry in the same harness-config mechanism, not a special test-only code path bolted on separately.\n\nSo concretely, the config that says \"harness equals Claude Code, invoke it via `claude -p`\" is structurally identical to a config that says \"harness equals fake, invoke it via `node fake-agent.js`,\" same interface, same expected output shape, JSON result object with usage, cost, session ID, whatever. {"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.31"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Overview

Thunderjar is a CLI benchmark that runs coding agents headlessly against a pinned codebase, measures what they produce, and keeps every run inspectable long after it finishes. It answers questions like "does prompt set `skills-v2` beat `skills-v1` on this task, with Haiku in Claude Code, at a 99% pass rate?"

**Goals**

- Compare harnesses, models and prompt sets on the same task from the same starting commit.
- Run many iterations of each combination and report pass rates, cost and tokens.
- Preserve each run so a developer can restore it months later and see exactly what the agent did.
- Let new measurements be applied to old runs without re-running the agent.
- Work in two modes: scripted CI, and interactive local exploration.

**Non-goals (for the proof of concept)**

- Infra retry/flakiness handling, cost previews and rate-limit governance (deferred nice-to-haves).
- Controlling sub-agent models. Only the harness's root model is a controlled variable; delegated models are observed.
- Multi-turn, steered tasks. Only one-shot-able tasks are Thunderjar candidates.

**Source of authority.** Decisions made in the design conversations are authoritative. The [repository](https://github.com/dwjohnston/thunderjar) is used for context only; where they disagree, this spec follows the conversation and notes the gap. The biggest gap: the repo isolates runs with git worktrees only, while this spec runs each iteration in a Docker container."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.32"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Terminology

The key split is type versus instance: a **measurer** is reusable evaluation logic, a **measurement** is one configured use of it on one task.

| Term | Definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task | A starting commit plus a task instruction, plus the measurements that judge it. Defines what the agent does and from what state. | `add-function` at commit `a1b2c3` |
| Task instruction | The text sent to the agent telling it what to do. Passed to harnesses as `ctx.taskInstruction`. | "Write a TypeScript function called `add`…" |
| Prompt set | A named, reusable action that shapes the agent's environment before the run (CLAUDE.md, skills, rules). Expressed as a shell command. Distinct from the task instruction. | `snerk`: copy `base_prompt_snerk.md` to `CLAUDE.md` |
| Harness | The agent tool, invoked headlessly via a `cli` callback. | `claude-code`, `opencode`, `cursor` |
| Model | The harness's root model. Sub-agent models are recorded, not controlled. | `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` |
| Experiment | A named comparison: one task plus variables. Produces one run per permutation. | `snerk-vs-glurk` |
| Variables | The swept axes of an experiment: harness, model, prompt set. | 1 harness × 1 model × 2 prompt sets = 2 runs |
| Run | One execution of a task under one permutation of variables. | `snerk / haiku / claude-code` |
| Iteration | One repeat of a run, used for pass-rate statistics. Each iteration gets its own container and ID. | iteration 37 of 100 |
| Measurer | Registered evaluation logic with a config type and a value type. Built-in or user-defined. | `grep`, `fileCreated`, `templateTest` |
| Measurement | A measurer plus a specific config, declared on a task. Copied per task, never shared by reference. | `grep` for `@ts-ignore` in `output/*.ts` |
| Measure | The value one measurement produced for one iteration: a `MeasurementResult<T>`. | `{ outcome: 'measured', data: false }` |
| Result | The set of measures for an iteration, keyed by measurement identity. Can grow after the run. | 3 measures at run time, 6 after a backfill |
| Standard outputs | Data captured from every iteration for free: final text block, commit list, changed-file diff, cost, tokens, duration. | `total_cost_usd: 0.021` |
| Content hash | A hash of the content that defines a prompt set, task instruction or measurement. Stored with the name to prove two runs are comparable. | `snerk@3f9a1c` |

`MeasurementResult<T>` is a measure, not a verdict:

```ts
type MeasurementResult<T> =
  | { outcome: 'measured'; data: T }
  | { outcome: 'skipped' }                           // could not be evaluated, e.g. no output existed
  | { outcome: 'erroredWhileMeasuring'; error: Error } // the measurer itself threw
```

Pass/fail is derived from a measure (for example `exitCode === expectedExitCode`), so numeric measures like token counts fit the same shape."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.33"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Core concepts

### Run identity

Two iterations are comparable only when every controlled input matches. A run's identity is the tuple below; iterations share it and differ only by iteration ID.

| Component | Recorded as | Controlled? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Resolved commit SHA (never the literal `HEAD`) | Yes |
| Task instruction | Task name + hash of the instruction text | Yes |
| Prompt set | Name + content hash | Yes |
| Harness | Name + version string (e.g. `claude --version`) | Yes |
| Model | Root model ID | Yes |
| Sub-agent models | Per-span model attribution from telemetry | No, observed outcome |

Measurements are deliberately not part of run identity. They describe how a run is judged, not how it was produced, so adding a measurement never invalidates past runs.

### Hash-based versioning

Files may be edited freely. Thunderjar never trusts a name alone; it records name plus content hash, and treats the pair as the true identity.

- **Prompt sets.** Hash the prompt set's folder (definition plus the content files it applies). `snerk@3f9a1c` and `snerk@d40e77` are different prompt sets that share a label; reports group and warn on this rather than silently merging them.
- **Measurements.** Identity = measurer name + hash of the measurer's source + hash of the canonical JSON config. Editing what a measurement checks produces a new identity; its old measures remain attached to the old identity.
- **Task instruction.** Hashed separately from the task's measurements, so appending measurements to a task file does not change the task's run identity.
- **Optional enforcement.** A later strict mode can refuse a run when a name's hash differs from a pinned hash. Detection is the default.

Determinism is the user's responsibility. A prompt set or setup command that calls a network API or reads the clock can produce different content under one hash. Thunderjar treats this as user error, not a framework concern.

### Measurements are copied, not shared

Each task owns its measurement configs outright. Shared named measurements (one `contains-ts-ignore` referenced by 30 tasks) were rejected: changing one would ripple through every task that uses it. If duplication becomes painful, a config-generating helper called at authoring time is acceptable, because the expanded config still lives inline in each task.

### Globs over exact filenames

Prefer broad globs (`output/*.ts`) for behavioural checks so agent naming choices (`isPrime.ts`, `is-prime.ts`) don't cause false failures. A specific filename in a glob is an implicit assertion that the agent named the file correctly; use it only when that is intended.

### Retroactive measurement (backfill)

Because every preserved iteration can be restored, new measurements can be evaluated against old runs without spending tokens. A result is an append-only map from measurement identity to measure: backfilling D, E and F adds three entries and leaves A, B and C untouched.

### Measurer authoring against a fixture

Writing a measurement is writing a test against a known filesystem state. The developer restores one finished iteration and iterates on the measurement locally until it is right, with no agent variance and no API cost. The agent run is the expensive fixture; it is produced once and reused."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.34"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## File structure

Configuration moves from one file to a folder per concept, so each prompt set, measurer and task is its own hashable unit.

### User project (the repo under test)

```text
my-repo/
├── thunderjar/
│   ├── thunderjar.config.ts        # configure(), harnesses, storage settings
│   ├── prompt-sets/
│   │   ├── snerk/                   # whole folder is hashed
│   │   │   ├── prompt-set.ts        # name + apply callback
│   │   │   └── CLAUDE.md
│   │   └── snerk-v2/
│   ├── measurers/                   # custom measurers only; built-ins ship with Thunderjar
│   │   └── dbRowCount.ts
│   ├── tasks/
│   │   ├── add-function.ts          # instruction, commit, inline measurements
│   │   └── is-prime/
│   │       ├── task.ts
│   │       └── is-prime.test.ts.template
│   ├── experiments/
│   │   └── snerk-vs-glurk.ts
│   └── mcp-fakes/                   # optional fake MCP servers for side-effect tasks
│       └── github.ts
└── .thunderjar/                     # gitignored, local-only
    ├── local.sqlite                 # local run metadata (ephemeral provenance)
    └── artifacts/<iterationId>/     # extracted lightweight artifacts
```

The repo's current layout (`evaluation-sandbox/thunderjar.config.ts` plus `prompts/*.md`, results in `bench/results/`) is the starting point; it migrates to the layout above.

### Thunderjar package

```text
thunderjar/
├── package.json                    # bin: thunderjar → src/cli/index.ts
├── src/
│   ├── cli/
│   │   ├── index.ts                # argument parsing and command routing
│   │   ├── commands/               # run, measure, backfill, list, restore, prune
│   │   └── tui/                    # ink components: RunnerDisplay, Explorer
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── ThunderJarConfig.ts     # builder API
│   │   ├── loadProject.ts          # discovers and loads the folders above
│   │   ├── hashing.ts              # content hashes for prompt sets, instructions, measurements
│   │   └── validate.ts             # e.g. experiment models ⊆ harness models
│   ├── engine/
│   │   ├── permutations.ts
│   │   ├── runIteration.ts         # the per-iteration pipeline
│   │   ├── standardOutputs.ts      # final text, commits, diff, cost, tokens
│   │   └── measure.ts              # evaluate measurements against a filesystem
│   ├── measurers/builtin/          # fileCreated, grep, commandExitCode, templateTest
│   ├── ports/                      # dependency-injection seams (interfaces)
│   │   ├── ContainerRuntime.ts
│   │   ├── MetadataStore.ts
│   │   └── ArtifactStore.ts
│   └── adapters/
│       ├── docker/                 # real container runtime + registry push/pull
│       ├── sqlite/                 # local metadata store
│       └── fake/                   # in-memory runtime and stores for tests
├── test/
│   ├── unit/
│   ├── integration/
│   └── fixtures/fake-harnesses/    # scripts that mimic harness output and edge cases
├── evaluation-sandbox/             # self-test project in the user-project layout
└── docs/
```"}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.36"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Run execution

Each iteration runs in its own Docker container, so iterations are isolated from each other and from the developer's workspace, and can run in parallel.

### Per-iteration pipeline

1. Resolve identity: commit SHA, prompt set hash, instruction hash, harness version. Mint an iteration ID (UUID).
2. Create a container from the base image. Copy the repo at the task commit into the container filesystem.
3. Run `onWorktreeCreate`, then the prompt set's `apply`, inside the container.
4. Start fake MCP servers if the task declares any.
5. Invoke the harness `cli` with telemetry env vars and a per-iteration cache namespace.
6. Capture standard outputs: harness JSON (`result`, `session_id`, `usage`, `total_cost_usd`), final text block, commit list with messages and hashes, diff against the task commit, duration.
7. Evaluate the task's measurements; store each measure keyed by measurement identity.
8. Extract lightweight artifacts: result JSON, OTel trace, session JSONL transcript, patch.
9. `docker commit` the container to an image tagged with the iteration ID, if the snapshot policy selects this iteration.
10. Record metadata; in CI, push the image and metadata to shared stores. Remove the container.

The code must live in the container's own filesystem, not a bind mount: `docker commit` does not capture bind-mounted volumes, so a mounted worktree would be missing from the snapshot.

### Cache isolation

The prompt cache lives on the provider's servers, so container isolation alone does not stop one iteration reusing another's cached prefix. Disabling caching (`DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING=1`) was rejected because caching within an iteration is realistic and cheap. The decided mechanism is a per-iteration cache namespace via Anthropic's prompt cache key, set to the iteration ID. Whether each harness CLI exposes a way to set it is an open question (see below).

### Telemetry

- Claude Code, Codex and Qwen Code support OpenTelemetry natively; OpenCode does not (community plugins only). For Claude Code: `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` plus `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`; tracing is beta.
- Cost from telemetry is API-equivalent pricing, not a subscription bill.
- Prefer `modelUsage` over `usage` when sub-agents are involved; plain `usage` undercounts.
- Thinking content is redacted from telemetry. Full reasoning is in the session JSONL transcript; `session_id` joins a trace span to its transcript file.
- Claude Code has no skill-invocation telemetry yet. Reconstruct skill use by matching SKILL.md paths in file-read tool calls.

### Credentials and side effects

Iterations must be side-effect free to be safely parallel. Real credentials that act externally (for example a GitHub token that can open PRs) are never passed into containers. Tasks that exercise an external flow declare a fake MCP server that records calls and returns canned responses; the `mcpCalls` measurer asserts on what was called. Model API keys are the only secrets a container receives."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

One engine, two front ends: scriptable commands for CI, and an interactive `explore` TUI for local work. Both call the same injected services, so both are equally testable.

| Command | Mode | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `thunderjar run <experiment…> [--iterations N] [--ci] [--json]` | Both | Runs experiments. Default 1 iteration; `--iterations 100` for confidence checks. `--ci` marks provenance and pushes to shared stores. Non-zero exit when a pass-rate threshold is missed. |
| `thunderjar measure <iterationId> [--task <file>]` | Local | Restores one iteration and evaluates the task's current measurements against it. The fast loop for authoring measurements. Results are not persisted unless `--save`. |
| `thunderjar backfill <task> [--measurement <id>]` | Both | Restores every preserved iteration of a task and evaluates measurements not yet recorded for it; appends measures. |
| `thunderjar list [experiments\|runs] [--local]` | Both | Lists config entries or stored runs; CI runs by default. |
| `thunderjar report <experiment> [--json]` | Both | Pass rates, cost and tokens per permutation, grouped by full identity; warns when one name has several hashes. |
| `thunderjar restore <iterationId>` | Local | Pulls the snapshot image and starts a container for VS Code Dev Containers to attach to. |
| `thunderjar prune [--older-than 30d] [--local]` | Both | Applies retention: removes images and artifacts past their tier's TTL. |
| `thunderjar explore` | Local | ink TUI: browse experiments → runs → iterations, view measures, trace and transcript, trigger restore or measure. |

The live run display follows the repo's paned-runner design: tiled ink panes per permutation, falling back to a list view when there are too many to tile. Harness output is captured, never written straight to the terminal."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.39"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Tooling used to build Thunderjar

Thunderjar is a Bun + TypeScript package with few dependencies; shell-outs go through `Bun.$`, as the repo already does.

| Concern | Choice | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runtime, package manager, test runner | Bun (repo built on 1.3.x; `bun test`) | In repo |
| Language and type checking | TypeScript 5, `tsc --noEmit` | In repo |
| Interactive prompts (current CLI) | `@inquirer/prompts` | In repo; superseded by ink for `explore` |
| TUI (run display, `explore`) | `ink` + React | Planned |
| Argument parsing | Not yet chosen (e.g. `commander` or Bun's `util.parseArgs`) | Open |
| Local metadata store | `bun:sqlite` (built in) | Planned |
| Shared metadata store | Postgres or S3 + manifest | Planned, CI only |
| Container runtime | Docker CLI via `Bun.$` behind a `ContainerRuntime` port | Planned |
| Hashing | SHA-256 via `Bun.CryptoHasher` | Planned |
| CI for Thunderjar itself | GitHub Actions: `oven-sh/setup-bun`, typecheck, test | In repo |
| Local telemetry backend (dev) | Any OTLP collector, e.g. Grafana + Tempo | Optional |

### Testing strategy

- **Unit tests (bulk of coverage).** Pure logic: permutation generation, validation, hashing, image-tag construction, parsing harness JSON into standard outputs, each built-in measurer against fixture directories.
- **Dependency-injected fakes.** `ContainerRuntime`, `MetadataStore` and `ArtifactStore` are interfaces with in-memory fakes, so the whole run pipeline and both CLI modes run without Docker or API calls.
- **Fake harnesses.** A fake harness is an ordinary harness entry (`cli: () => 'bun fake-agent.ts'`), not a test-only code path. Fixture scripts cover edge cases: never commits, malformed JSON, times out, writes outside `output/`.
- **A few real integration tests.** Run a trivial container end to end against a real Docker daemon to prove `commit`, tagging and restore work. Registry push is lower priority.
- **Dogfooding.** `evaluation-sandbox/` stays a self-contained project in the user layout, exercised with the fake harness in CI and real harnesses locally."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

A user needs Bun, git and Docker locally; harness CLIs run inside the agent base image, not on the host.

| Tool | Needed for | Required? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bun ≥ 1.2 | Running the Thunderjar CLI and TypeScript config | Yes |
| git | Resolving task commits, diffs, commit lists | Yes |
| Docker Engine (or compatible, e.g. OrbStack, Colima) | Iteration containers, snapshots, restore | Yes |
| Model provider credentials (e.g. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, OpenCode or Cursor auth) | Passed into containers for the harnesses under test | Yes, per harness used |
| Agent base image with harness CLIs (`claude`, `opencode`, Cursor `agent`) | Running harnesses in containers; built once from a Thunderjar-provided Dockerfile | Yes |
| Harness CLIs on the host | Only for `--no-container` debugging, matching today's worktree mode | Optional |
| Container registry access (e.g. AWS ECR) | Pushing and pulling CI snapshots | CI; optional locally |
| VS Code + Dev Containers extension | Attaching to a restored iteration to browse files and git history | Optional |
| OTLP collector (e.g. Grafana + Tempo) | Viewing traces live | Optional |

Harness versions are pinned by the base image tag, which makes harness version a reproducible part of run identity."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

input.payload:
{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.41"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## User flows

Seven flows cover the tool end to end: lifecycle, task creation, the per-iteration pipeline, measurement authoring, backfill, CI, and explore/restore. A data model diagram closes the section.

### 1. Lifecycle overview

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Everyday agent work"] --> B{"One-shot-able?"}
  B -- "No: needed steering" --> X["Not a Thunderjar task"]
  B -- "Yes" --> C["Create task + measurements"]
  C --> D["Fast loop: 1 iteration"]
  D --> E{"Prompt and measurements right?"}
  E -- "No" --> F["Edit prompt set or measurement"]
  F --> D
  E -- "Yes" --> G["Confidence loop: 50-100 iterations"]
  G --> H{"Pass rate met?"}
  H -- "No" --> F
  H -- "Yes" --> I["Commit config, CI runs it"]
  I --> J["Canonical results + snapshots"]
  J --> K["Explore, report, backfill"]
```

### 2. Creating a task from real work

Follows the repo's regular-usage workflow: mine measurements from a known-good change, then pin a commit that has the measurements but not the solution.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Commit A: before the change"] --> B["Commits B..D: agent-assisted solution"]
  B --> C["Mine measurements from A..D diff"]
  C --> D["Commit E: task file + test templates"]
  D --> F["Branch from A, cherry-pick E"]
  F --> G["Tip SHA becomes task commitHash"]
  C --> H{"What did the human have to add?"}
  H -- "Convention gap" --> I["Keep instruction; iterate prompt sets"]
  H -- "Specification gap" --> J["Rewrite task instruction"]
```

### 3. Per-iteration pipeline

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  actor Dev as Developer or CI
  participant CLI as thunderjar run
  participant Eng as Engine
  participant RT as ContainerRuntime
  participant H as Harness in container
  participant MS as MetadataStore
  participant AS as Artifact store and registry
  Dev->>CLI: run experiment --iterations N
  CLI->>Eng: load folders, validate, hash, build permutations
  loop each permutation x iteration
    Eng->>RT: create container from base image
    Eng->>RT: copy repo at task commit
    Eng->>RT: onWorktreeCreate, apply prompt set, start MCP fakes
    Eng->>H: invoke cli with telemetry env and cache key
    H-->>Eng: result JSON, exit code
    Eng->>RT: collect commits, diff, transcript, trace
    Eng->>RT: evaluate measurements
    Eng->>AS: store lightweight artifacts
    alt snapshot policy selects iteration
      Eng->>RT: docker commit, tag with iteration ID
      Eng->>AS: push image (CI only)
    end
    Eng->>MS: write iteration record
    Eng->>RT: remove container
  end
  Eng-->>CLI: summary
  CLI-->>Dev: report, exit code
```

### 4. Authoring a measurement against a fixture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Run task once with a real harness"] --> B["Iteration preserved"]
  B --> C["thunderjar measure iterationId"]
  C --> D["Restore snapshot, evaluate current task measurements"]
  D --> E{"Measurement behaves as intended?"}
  E -- "No" --> F["Edit glob, pattern or test template"]
  F --> C
  E -- "Yes" --> G["Commit task file; measurement hash recorded"]
  G --> H["Optionally backfill older runs"]
```

No tokens are spent inside the loop; only step A calls a model.

### 5. Backfilling new measurements

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  actor Dev as Developer
  participant CLI as thunderjar backfill
  participant MS as MetadataStore
  participant AS as Registry
  participant RT as ContainerRuntime
  Dev->>CLI: backfill task
  CLI->>MS: find preserved iterations of task
  CLI->>CLI: compute measurement identities D, E, F
  loop each iteration missing D, E or F
    CLI->>AS: pull snapshot image
    CLI->>RT: start container read-only
    CLI->>RT: evaluate missing measurements only
    CLI->>MS: append measures; A, B, C untouched
    CLI->>RT: remove container
  end
  CLI-->>Dev: pass rates now include D, E, F
```

Iterations without a snapshot can only be backfilled for measurements that work from lightweight artifacts (patch, transcript, final text).

### 6. CI run

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Push or PR"] --> B["CI job: setup Bun, pull base image"]
  B --> C["thunderjar run --ci --json"]
  C --> D["Iterations in parallel"]
  D --> E["Records to shared metadata store"]
  D --> F["Snapshots to registry"]
  E --> G{"Pass-rate thresholds met?"}
  G -- "Yes" --> H["Exit 0"]
  G -- "No" --> I["Exit non-zero, JSON summary"]
  J["Scheduled prune"] --> F
```

### 7. Explore and restore

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["thunderjar explore"] --> B["Experiments list, CI runs by default"]
  B -- "toggle" --> B2["Include local runs"]
  B --> C["Permutations with pass rate, cost, tokens"]
  C --> D["Iterations"]
  D --> E["Measures + standard outputs"]
  E --> F{"Need more?"}
  F -- "Telemetry view" --> G["Trace + session transcript via session_id"]
  F -- "Full restore" --> H["Pull image, start container"]
  H --> I["Attach VS Code Dev Containers, browse files and git"]
  F -- "Try a measurement" --> J["thunderjar measure"]
```

### Data model

```mermaid
erDiagram
  EXPERIMENT ||--o{ RUN : "one per permutation"
  TASK ||--o{ EXPERIMENT : "is compared by"
  TASK ||--|{ MEASUREMENT : "declares inline"
  MEASURER ||--o{ MEASUREMENT : "is configured by"
  RUN ||--|{ ITERATION : "repeats"
  ITERATION ||--o{ MEASURE : "append-only"
  MEASUREMENT ||--o{ MEASURE : "produces"
  ITERATION ||--o| SNAPSHOT : "may have"
  ITERATION ||--|| ARTIFACTS : "always has"
  RUN {
    string commitSha
    string instructionHash
    string promptSetName
    string promptSetHash
    string harness
    string harnessVersion
    string model
  }
  MEASUREMENT {
    string measurerName
    string measurerHash
    string configHash
  }
  ITERATION {
    string iterationId
    string provenance
    float costUsd
  }
```"}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.42"]}, "with": {"from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "## Risks, open questions and deferred work

### Known risks

- **Hidden non-determinism.** A setup or prompt-set command that reads the network or clock breaks the "same hash, same content" promise without any visible signal. Accepted as user error.
- **Snapshot fidelity.** `docker commit` captures files, not running processes, and not bind mounts. A measurement that needs a service (a database, a dev server) must restart it after restore. Measurements that install dependencies at evaluation time can drift months later; pin the base image by digest and keep test templates self-contained.
- **Snapshot coverage.** With the default policy, passing iterations have no snapshot, so backfill on them is limited to measurements that read lightweight artifacts. Use `snapshot: 'all'` for tasks where backfill matters.

### Open questions

- [ ] Can each harness CLI set a per-iteration prompt cache key? If a CLI cannot pass custom request headers, it needs a proxy or a different isolation approach.
- [ ] Harness–model representation: keep nested `harnesses: { name: models[] }` or move to explicit `agents: [{ harness, model }]` pairs (see the repo's harness-vs-models note)?
- [ ] Should prompt set identity also include a hash of the files actually changed by `apply`, to catch content outside the prompt set folder?
- [ ] `templateTest` details: placeholder substitution, default `run` command, cleanup of generated tests, working directory.
- [ ] On a second trigger in the same session, does a harness re-read an already-loaded skill file or rely on context? Affects skill-usage reconstruction.
- [ ] Argument parser choice for the scripted CLI.
- [ ] How to spot good task candidates during everyday work: a hook that nudges, or a skill the user invokes?

### Reconciling the current repo

| Repo today | This spec |
| --- | --- |
| Git worktree per run, removed after the run | Container per iteration, snapshotted by policy |
| `commitHash` on the experiment, often `'HEAD'` | Commit on the task, resolved to a full SHA |
| Single config file | Folders per prompt set, measurer, task, experiment |
| Prompt set name only | Name + content hash |
| Results as JSON files in `bench/results/` | SQLite locally; shared stores in CI |
| Experiment models not checked against harness models | Validated at load time |
| Raw ANSI progress display | ink paned display |

### Deferred (nice-to-have after the proof of concept)

- Retry and flakiness handling for Thunderjar's own Docker and registry calls, separate from real measurement failures.
- Cost preview and rate-limit governance before large batches.
- Strict mode that pins hashes and refuses drifted prompt sets or measurements.
- Published measurer packs (for example database assertions)."}, "as": "markdown"}}]}

{"ops": [{"op": "insert", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.52"]}, "side": "after", "source": {"as": "markdown", "from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "**Motivations**

A coding agent's behaviour is a non-deterministic function of four things: codebase state (C), prompt configuration (P, including AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, skills and the task instruction), model (M) and harness (H). Thunderjar holds three fixed and varies one, so a change in outcome can be attributed. Background: [Does this tool exist?](https://blacksheepcode.com/posts/coding_agent_testing) (Black Sheep Code, July 2026).

- **Diagnosing regressions.** Prompts that work today may perform worse in six months. Re-running a banked task isolates the cause: re-run old C + old P on today's M and H to test for model or harness drift; run today's P on old C to test for prompt bloat; run old P on today's C to test whether the codebase changed.
- **De-risking a switch.** Before changing model or harness (for example Claude Code to OpenCode, or Sonnet to a cheaper model), run the same tasks with only that variable changed and compare pass rate, cost and tokens.
- **Measuring prompt techniques.** Advice like "use skills", "use sub-agents" or "keep one big session" is untested until it is measured, the same way a performance fix is unproven without a benchmark.
- **Tracking cost and speed.** Token consumption, cost and duration are hard to see in most providers' tooling; Thunderjar records them per iteration alongside correctness."}}}]}

input.payload:
{"ops": [{"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.4350"]}, "ifRev": 14, "with": {"as": "markdown", "from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "| Component | Recorded as | Controlled? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code | Resolved commit SHA (never the literal `HEAD`) | Yes |
| Base image | Image digest (`sha256:…`), not a mutable tag; covers OS, runtimes such as Node or Bun, and harness CLIs | Yes |
| Task instruction | Task name + hash of the instruction text | Yes |
| Prompt set | Name + content hash | Yes |
| Harness | Name + version string (e.g. `claude --version`) | Yes |
| Model | Root model ID | Yes |
| Sub-agent models | Per-span model attribution from telemetry | No, observed outcome |"}}}, {"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.14736"]}, "ifRev": 14, "with": {"as": "markdown", "from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "1. Resolve identity: commit SHA, base image digest, prompt set hash, instruction hash, harness version. Mint an iteration ID (UUID).
2. Build or reuse the **start image** for this permutation: the base image (by digest), plus the repo at the task commit, plus `onWorktreeCreate`, plus the prompt set's `apply`. This is exactly what the agent sees. It is always preserved and tagged, and every iteration of the permutation shares it, so it costs one layer per permutation, not per iteration.
3. Start a container from the start image. Start fake MCP servers if the task declares any.
4. Invoke the harness `cli` with telemetry env vars and a per-iteration cache namespace.
5. Capture standard outputs: harness JSON (`result`, `session_id`, `usage`, `total_cost_usd`), final text block, commit list with messages and hashes, diff against the task commit, duration.
6. Evaluate the task's measurements; store each measure keyed by measurement identity.
7. Extract lightweight artifacts: result JSON, OTel trace, session JSONL transcript, patch.
8. `docker commit` the finished container to an **end image** tagged with the iteration ID, if the snapshot policy selects this iteration.
9. Record metadata; in CI, push images and metadata to shared stores. Remove the container."}}}, {"op": "replace", "target": {"kind": "blocks", "ids": ["mv7z9mz74gt.30273"]}, "ifRev": 14, "with": {"as": "markdown", "from": {"kind": "inline", "content": "- **Hidden non-determinism.** A setup or prompt-set command that reads the network or clock breaks the "same hash, same content" promise without any visible signal. Accepted as user error.
- **Environment drift is solved by containers.** Measurements and backfills run inside the iteration's own preserved image, so they see the original runtime even years later. Runs on different base image digests (for example a Node minor bump) are not strictly comparable: reports group by digest, and comparing across digests is opt-in. To test today's measurement fairly against an old run, re-run it on that run's preserved start image.
- **What a snapshot misses.** `docker commit` captures files, not running processes or bind mounts. A measurement that needs a service (a database, a dev server) must restart it after restore.
- **Snapshot coverage.** With the default policy, passing iterations have no end image, so backfill on them is limited to measurements that read lightweight artifacts. Use `snapshot: 'all'` for tasks where backfill matters. Start images are always kept."}}}]}
